evidence.quote: clonally propagated trees often begin to bear during the first year after planting.
evidence.doc: World Agroforestry (ICRAF), Agroforestree Database 4.0 (Orwa et al. 2009), Psidium guajava species sheet

yearsToFirstCrop.notes: International ICRAF reference for clonally propagated stock only: trees often begin bearing during the first year after planting. The seedling timing in the source concerns flowering, so no seed-grown first fruit age is assigned. This is not confirmed for South African sites.

evidence.quote: Trees reach full bearing after 5-8 years, depending on growing conditions and spacing. The guava is not a long-lived tree (about 40 years), but the plants may bear heavily for 15-25 years.
evidence.doc: World Agroforestry (ICRAF), Agroforestree Database 4.0 (Orwa et al. 2009), Psidium guajava species sheet

yearsToFullBearing.notes: International ICRAF reference; growing conditions and spacing affect full bearing. This is not a South African site forecast.

evidence.quote: Average yields are between 30-40 kg/plant in 5 year-old plants and will reach a maximum production of 50-70 kg at about 7 years if well managed.
evidence.doc: World Agroforestry (ICRAF), Agroforestree Database 4.0 (Orwa et al. 2009), Psidium guajava species sheet

yieldKgPerTreeMature.notes: ICRAF's international species reference reports maximum production of 50–70 kg/plant at about 7 years under good management; at age 5 it reports 30–40 kg/plant. These are not South Africa-specific farm forecasts. Match plant age, cultivar, site and care before applying this reference.

evidence.quote: In the subtropics quiescent trees withstand light frost and 3.5-6 months (depending on the cultivar) of mean temperatures above 16 deg. C suffice for flowering and fruiting.
evidence.doc: World Agroforestry (ICRAF), Agroforestree Database 4.0 (Orwa et al. 2009), Psidium guajava species sheet

chillUnits.notes: This describes a WARMTH requirement (months above 16°C) for flowering, not a winter-chill/dormancy requirement, and guava is evergreen/subtropical with no known formal chill-unit requirement; left null rather than 0 because no source frames it in chill-unit terms.

evidence.quote: Bees are the principal pollinators. There is some self- and cross-incompatibility but several cultivars have set fair crops of seedless or few-seeded fruit. Levels of 60-75% selfing have been found in natural populations; this has been used to produce homozygotic varieties that can be propagated from seed.
evidence.doc: World Agroforestry (ICRAF), Agroforestree Database 4.0 (Orwa et al. 2009), Psidium guajava species sheet

pollination.notes: Guava is capable of substantial self-pollination (60-75% selfing measured in natural populations) but also benefits from bee-mediated cross-pollination and shows some self-incompatibility in certain cultivars, matching 'partly-self-fertile' rather than a clean 'self-fertile' or 'needs-cross-pollinator'. Not South Africa-specific.

gaps: NEMBA (National Environmental Management: Biodiversity Act) official invasive-species listing CONFIRMED via direct fetch of the Government Gazette PDF: '293. Psidium guajava L. Guava a. 2 for plantations in Eastern Cape, KwaZulu-Natal, Limpopo, Mpumalanga and North-West. b. 3 elsewhere in Eastern Cape, Kwazulu-Natal, Limpopo, Mpumalanga and North-West. c. The fruit of the guava is not listed if used for human consumption.' (source: https://enviroworx.co.za/wp-content/uploads/2022/11/NEMBA-Invasive-Species-Lists-July-2016.pdf, a hosted copy of the DFFE/Government Gazette 'Alien and Invasive Species Lists' under NEMBA, GN R.864/1003, item 293, page 20 of the PDF; the official dffe.gov.za-hosted copy returned HTTP 503 on direct fetch). This is Category 2 for guava PLANTATIONS in the five named provinces (permit-controlled commercial cultivation) and Category 3 elsewhere in those provinces (no new planting, but existing plants may generally remain), with fruit for human consumption explicitly excluded from the listing.

No South Africa-specific harvest-month data could be verified: ARC-ITSC's own guava page (arc.agric.za/arc-itsc/Pages/Guava.aspx) returned HTTP 503 on every attempt; a relevant peer-reviewed South African Journal of Plant and Soil article ('Preliminary evaluation of guava selections for guava wilt disease resistance in South Africa') was found but is paywalled (HTTP 403) on Tandfonline; agribook.co.za's guava/subtropical-fruit pages gave production-volume and processing-vs-fresh-market figures but no harvest calendar. harvestMonths left as an empty array rather than filled with an unverified figure.

All quantitative bearing-age, yield-per-tree and pollination data used here come from a single global (non-South-African) source, the World Agroforestry Agroforestree Database; no South African primary source (ARC-ITSC, DAFF/DALRRD, or a specific SA guava growers' body) could be reached to confirm, refine or replace these figures for South African cultivars (e.g. 'Fan Retief', 'TS-G2') or conditions.

Confirmed South African guava production-region figures exist (Western Cape 547 ha, Limpopo 442 ha, Mpumalanga 140 ha, per a ResearchGate figure caption from 'Advances in Guava Propagation') but the underlying paper was not independently fetched to confirm the figures verbatim or find associated yield/bearing data, so not used as evidence.
